newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Budget vote is European Parliament's hour of glory.
newsitem.headline: Budget vote is European Parliament's hour of glory.

text.p: The European Parliament, an assembly often derided as a mere talking shop, meets this week to vote on the European Union's budget, a moment in the sun when it can really make its voice heard.

The 628 deputies representing almost 100 political parties from the 15 EU states will devote their monthly session in the French city of Strasbourg to the draft 88 billion European currency unit ($109.7 billion) budget for 1997.
Despite differences of political affiliation and national background, the Euro-MPs hope for a show of strength against EU member states and the European Commission.

"We use the budget as our instrument of policy," Detlev Samland, head of the parliament's budgetary committee, told Reuters in an interview. "A parliament is not handed rights, it has to fight for its rights."

Such rights have been given sparingly to the EU's only directly elected body by national governments -- it cannot, for example, initiate legislation -- but the annual budget exercise gives it some clout.
It has no control to earmark farm spending, roughly half of the Union's expenditure, but it can reject the budget as a whole -- and has done so twice, in 1979 and 1984.
It also has project-by-project control over funds for the interior and exterior policies of the Union, for administration, and for regional aid.

"In practical terms there is almost no realm of politics where you don't have to spend money," Samland said. "The budget is our instrument. We get our way if we manage to get 314 people (the majority in the parliament) behind us."

During the three-day budget debate, the parliament will try to find additional funds for the trans-European networks, 14 giant projects of rail and road infrastructure launched by EU leaders three years ago to help create jobs.
EU finance ministers, concerned about national budget constraints, last week blocked new funding of one billion Ecus that the Commission had hoped would jump-start the projects.

Samland said the parliament would be asked to vote on making the money available after all. Part of it would have to come from savings, he said, but the Socialists, the assembly's biggest grouping, would also vote to increase the budget.
One of the parliament's most effective instruments -- the power to freeze funding for projects -- will also be on display.

In the area of external relations, the parliament will seek to block all projects for Turkey, apart from those seeking to improve democracy and human rights, and those designed to improve living conditions for Turks of Kurdish origin.
Samland's budgetary committee has also approved a proposal to freeze half the 45 million Ecu budget for the Commission's department responsible for information policy.
Euro-MPs have charged that the department is ineffective. If they approve the plan this week, the money would be put into reserve until the department is reorganised.

And earlier this month, the budget committee even went as far as threatening to cut EU commissioners' 1997 salaries if they did not reorganise the Commission's department responsible for tourism, which is subject to allegations of mismanagement.
The department's chief was asked to take early retirement last week, although the Commission said the request was in no way linked to the committee's threat.
"For three years we asked them to (act) and nothing ever happened," Samland said. "Now we threaten them with freezing the salaries and bingo -- they react within days."
